content: Interactions within a digital health system should be categorized as inputs, outputs, or outcomes. This classification is essential for guiding the management team in selecting and measuring input indicators to be included in monitoring activities. To begin this process, it is critical to ask whether the user is a primary or secondary user. Primary users are those who directly interact with the digital health system, such as health workers or clients. For example, they may enter information into a digital health application and transmit the data, rely on a digital health algorithm to assess a client’s risk for specific illnesses, or send SMS messages to learn about contraception methods. Secondary users, on the other hand, passively interact with the system. For instance, they may receive SMS reminders to take their medication or visit a healthcare facility, receive phone calls educating them about hygienic practices, or get SMS reminders to visit specific clients in rural areas. The inputs measured in a digital health intervention vary depending on the type of intervention and how targeted users interact with the system. Identifying whether the user is primary or secondary is the first step in determining the technical and user-linked inputs of the intervention. For primary users, technical and user inputs are often intertwined, making it challenging to separate them when monitoring fidelity and quality components of the intervention. In some implementations, both primary and secondary users may be involved, requiring a nuanced approach to monitoring. For example, the outcomes of an intervention might include metrics such as 90% of immunization reminder messages being read by the target family within one day of delivery or a 30% increase in polio vaccine coverage in a specific area. Detailed guidance on evaluating output and outcome indicators specific to digital health system interactions can be found in Chapter 4 on Evaluation. Implementers of digital health systems must ensure that inputs are of the highest quality. In non-digital health interventions, this might involve providing high-quality training, evidence-based behavior change communication messaging, or high-quality supplements with the expected nutrient content. Similarly, in digital health projects, high-quality inputs—such as adequate training to support worker performance or effective sanitation and hand-washing message content—are critical to the intervention’s success. Unlike non-digital interventions, additional monitoring is required to ensure that the digital health application, support systems, and users meet specified standards and are ready for deployment and sustained use. When setting up a monitoring plan, it is also important to determine the maturity stage of the intervention. This assessment allows project teams to allocate time and resources appropriately. Early-stage projects should invest heavily in ensuring the system is functional and stable, while more advanced projects may focus on quality and performance monitoring, scaling up, and continuous improvements. Interventions in a middle stage of maturity may require significant upgrades to pilot-tested technology to make it more robust and user-friendly, while also addressing new considerations such as standardization of training and systematic day-to-day monitoring. Monitoring burdens differ across maturity stages. Early-stage interventions have a higher burden of technical monitoring (e.g., functionality and stability), while later-stage interventions focus more on implementation-linked monitoring (e.g., fidelity and quality). Monitoring components include functionality (ensuring the system operates as intended), stability (ensuring consistent operation), fidelity (assessing whether field realities alter the system’s intended functionality), and quality (evaluating the content and delivery of the intervention). To support monitoring, several tools and processes are essential. These include human-centered design (HCD), software requirements specification (SRS), use case narratives, wireframes, quality assurance (QA) test cases, data, codebooks, indicator lists, and dashboards. HCD focuses on designing systems with the needs and limitations of end-users in mind, improving both the quality and fidelity of the intervention. The SRS outlines the technical requirements of the system, serving as a reference document throughout development and testing. Use cases describe how target users perform specific tasks using the technology, while wireframes provide schematic illustrations of the system’s expected functionality. QA test cases break down system functionality into discrete steps, allowing implementation teams to verify whether expected actions occur as intended. Data management is critical, and programme teams must ensure that the data needed for monitoring and evaluation is available, complete, and usable. Codebooks provide detailed descriptions of data elements, ensuring clear communication between development and programme teams. Indicator lists outline the key metrics to be monitored and evaluated, serving as a roadmap for the monitoring plan. Finally, data dashboards organize and present information in a way that facilitates interpretation and decision-making. Dashboards can display high-priority indicators by time point, worker, location, or summary overview, reducing the burden of report generation and enabling real-time, data-driven decisions. Visualizations on dashboards help project managers quickly understand system and worker performance, which may not be immediately apparent in tabular formats.
